When I was growing up, this was one of the things that I was taught. Good advice, too(a bit of a rarity, people have given kids a lot of shit advice all throughout history). I try not to speak for anyone except myself unless someone has specifically told me to speak on their behalf.

In the past 20 years or so, however, I've seen the usage of the word "we", go from an occasional journalistic affectation, to an almost constant echo in the dialogue of millions. The constant implication of speaking for an entire group seems to have become an accepted part of discussion, despite the massive claims of knowledge this entails. I'm personally quite sure that the internet had some effect on this, with the dissolving of traditional journalism and blogging together. But I think that there are several other factors that may have presaged this.

First is the constant teaching to avoid using the word "I" in schools. Even back when I went to school, recurrent use of the word "I" was criticized, and kids would often be called selfish and uncaring if they used the word too often. There are some seriously negative consequences to this, IMO. One of them being the usage of replacement words that do not mean the same thing, but which on some level are intended to carry the same message. This results in linguistic confusion, confusing not just the reader, but also the writer of their own intent. These constant demands to avoid writing of oneself as an single individual may have in some way contributed to the identity politics riven culture that exists today.

As a bit of anecdotal backup to this, I was speaking to a man who was arguing with some anti-gentrification protestors a while ago. They claimed that it would help him feel more empathetic if he used to word "we". Personally, I think it would do the opposite.

Please, anytime you think of using the word "we", or "us", or any other group terms, please stop, and think for a moment. Who is "we" other than yourself? Who is this "us" you claim to speak for?
